cap: Cervical screening rules follow how slowly HPV lesions progress. Cytology alone starts at 21 and repeats every 3 years until 29; from 30 to 65 primary HPV testing or a cotest every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years, is used. Screening stops after 65 with adequate negative results or after total hysterectomy for benign disease, but never for people with HIV. A screening test only sorts risk; colposcopy with biopsy diagnoses, and excision treats high-grade lesions. The 9-valent vaccine prevents infection but does not replace screening.
teach: Read the top grid as a decision by age and risk, then the middle row as the three separate jobs in cancer prevention: screen, diagnose, treat. A cervix that is still present keeps its transformation zone, so a supracervical hysterectomy does not end screening, while a total hysterectomy for benign disease does. Excision of the transformation zone treats precancer but removes supportive stroma, so conization carries the greatest risk of later cervical insufficiency. The vaccine contains L1 capsid protein only, so it cannot cause infection and cannot clear an existing one.
